Chapter Twenty-Eight


Arthur pulled the condom off his softening cock and marveled at the woman in the bed before him. She was all soft edges, swells, and curves, like a goddess in a painting. Her still-damp auburn hair fanned behind her on the pillow, and she had a sleepy, satisfied look on her face that he had given her. Fuck.


He hated to leave her, even for a second, but they both needed something to eat. It had been so long since they ate leftovers at the campsite that morning. He filled a glass with water and then looked for something that wouldn’t make too much of a mess, deciding on a bag of grapes.


When he returned to the bedroom, Maggie half opened her eyes. “I see you’ve gone foraging.”


“You need to eat.” He arranged the grapes and water on her nightstand, gently pushing a stack of books to the side. “But I’m not very interested in getting out of this bed.”


She opened her eyes completely, and her gaze turned sharp with lust. “Me neither.”


He slid alongside Maggie beneath her thin quilt, and she tucked herself in next to him, resting her head on his chest as he leaned back against the stacked pillows. For a moment, he thought they might fall asleep like this, even though it was still the afternoon, based on the light coming through Maggie’s windows.


They lay in silence, Maggie lazily eating one and then two grapes, but Arthur found he wasn’t hungry. He kept being sidetracked by Maggie. Neither of them had bothered putting clothes back on, and it was very distracting—the brush of Maggie’s thigh against his hip, her breasts pressed into his torso as she leaned over him to grab another pillow, the lavender scent of her soap mingling with the smell of their bodies.


A thought kept coming to Arthur that he couldn’t shake, but it wasn’t one he should be having. Not now. Not when he knew that Maggie was terrified of their relationship turning into something more. But he couldn’t believe how comfortable this was. How easy. Even the friction between them, their disagreements, their jabs, were like a well-worn sweater. And he didn’t know what that would mean if Maggie decided to run from it like she had on Beltane.


After a while, Maggie said in a small, quiet voice, “We should talk about the rules.”


“Rules?” Arthur asked, his stomach sinking slightly. She rested her head on his chest and turned to look up at him, her dark brown eyes impossibly large.


She hesitated, biting her lip. “You are still my colleague,” she said. “My office mate! Not to mention, there are a lot of people counting on us…on you, to remove the pall. Things need to stay professional.”


“Of course,” he said, a little relieved. He knew how Maggie’s methodical mind worked. All Diadhan linguists had a streak of wanting to make the unquantifiable quantified, the unknowable known, and Maggie was no different. Alchemists had the same predisposition, but even Arthur knew there were some things in this world that still defied logic. “We’ve been nothing but professional so far,” he added.


She snorted. “I’m serious,” she pleaded.


“Okay, okay. Tell me your rules.”


“I don’t date other professors,” she began, and he cocked an eyebrow. “Before you say ‘we’re not dating’ ”—even through his uncertainty he smiled because she had read him like a book—“let me just add that I don’t sleep with other professors either.”


“Oh, so you’re a rebel. Already breaking your own rules.”


“Technically, neither of us are teaching classes right now.”


“Nothing like succeeding on a technicality,” he teased. If this was how she needed to justify it to herself, Arthur would let her. He didn’t mind. At least that was what he kept telling himself.


But Arthur’s gut twisted when she continued. “That means this has to be over when classes start again.” She said it so firmly, like there was no room to discuss it. No chance to change her mind.


Even Arthur had to admit that dating Maggie outside of this summer would be complicated. He understood where she was coming from, he did, but he hated the idea of ending whatever was sparking between them before it had a chance to catch fire. Seven more weeks—that’s how long he would have to convince her that whatever this was, it was worth breaking her rules for.


Arthur’s throat bobbed as he swallowed, and his jaw tensed for the first time since she’d told him about Evan at the campsite. She looked at him expectantly, but he couldn’t make himself say yes out loud, so he just nodded. “What else?” he managed to ask.


“We can’t let this distract us from dissipating the pall.” That, at least, he agreed with. As much as he hated the idea of eventually leaving this bed and Maggie’s apartment, he was itching to get back into the lab to start the gloaming creeper decoction. After all, their idea that the plant could amplify their spellwork and cancel out the confluence was just a theory. What if it didn’t work?


Maggie went on. “And we can’t tell anyone.”


He tilted his head and smirked at her. “You’re telling me you didn’t already text Dahlia when I was in the kitchen?”


Her face turned red, her skin hot against his chest. “Are you snooping on my phone?”


He chuckled. “You’re just predictable, Maggie.”


She pretended to be shocked, dropping her perfect lips in a round O. “That might be the most offensive thing you’ve ever said to me.”


“Give me a few weeks,” he said. “I can think of a few particularly filthy things I’d like to say to you that some might call offensive.”


His words had the desired effect. Her narrowed eyes softened with lust, and she leaned up to kiss him. The kiss was slow and smooth as they grew more acquainted with the topography of each other’s lips, with the way they liked to move together. He knew he would never tire of her sweet taste on his mouth or her skin against his.


When she finally broke the kiss, she leaned back on his chest, and he held her close to him. “Fine. I did tell Dahlia. But she doesn’t count.”


“Then I’ll tell Rory and we’ll be even.” He sighed. “So I get you for seven weeks?”


“Seven weeks,” she said, her gaze distant as she began tracing looping whorls on his stomach with her finger, sending a pleasurable chill through him that was much better than the worry that had returned with a force.



—


Arthur didn’t leave Maggie’s apartment until the next morning. It had taken them both significant willpower to admit that Arthur needed to return to the bungalow in Atlantia to change his clothes and then return to campus so they could meet up again at their reserved lab space, but eventually they had pulled themselves apart. Arthur had left Maggie with a long, languid kiss at her front door.


The roads to Atlantia were winding, crisscrossing over the marshlands and estuaries that marked this part of the coast, and he had plenty of time to think. Images of their night in the Wilds, of the day they had spent locked in Maggie’s apartment, struck him again and again, and his cock hardened as he thought of his tongue inside her, of the way she had worked him with her hands and mouth. He needed to get this out of his system, or it was going to be impossible to work together side by side in the quiet, empty lab.


The bungalow was, thank the gods below, empty. His father and Rory were both in the field today and had gotten early starts, leaving the remnants of their hurried breakfast on the table. Arthur would clean it up before he went back to Hawthorn, but first he walked into his bedroom and lay on the bed. He slid his hands beneath the waistband of his pants and began stroking himself, thinking of the way Maggie had opened for him, had come for him, had made him lose himself completely with her touch, her smell, her taste. It was seconds before he was coming. He leaned back, cursing, staring up at the same ceiling he’d stared at many times after doing this exact same thing on sticky, hot summer nights.


Seven weeks. Seven. It was going to go too fast; he knew that without a doubt. Time was speeding past, and he would do what he could to spend every minute of it with Maggie, but it would never be enough. He had lied to Maggie in the Wilds. She had asked him if he was afraid of the force of what he felt between them and he had said no, but the truth was that it terrified him. Not how fast and how hard he was falling, but how uncertain he was that she would ever get to the point of letting this turn into something real. He would have to be satisfied with seven weeks. Or he would have to try to change her mind.


Arthur showered and changed, hesitating only a moment before throwing a backpack with spare clothes into the back seat of his car. There was nothing wrong with being prepared and avoiding another trek out to Atlantia when he didn’t need to. Before he left, he cleaned up his brother and father’s breakfast mess and left a good-luck note for Simon. He had only a couple more practices before his big, final baseball game.


Arthur wondered idly if Maggie would think it was weird if he invited her to go with him to a five-year-old’s baseball game. They had a seven-week expiration date…should they go to family functions together? Probably not, but Arthur had no idea what he was doing. Not with any of it. Unfortunately, the drive back to Galloway gave him plenty of time to think.


He had not gone to the bonfire intending to hook up with anyone and had surprised himself completely when he’d kissed the woman by the shore. He hadn’t been thinking about Maggie at all that night, not after she’d so clearly been avoiding him. The possibility of anything happening with Maggie Linden had been nothing but a daydream, so he’d given in to the kiss, knowing he’d never see the woman again. And now…had he always known, somehow, that it was her?


Back on campus, they were meant to meet in the botany lab in Ulmus, but Arthur needed to stop at Ferox Hall first. Before he’d left Atlantia, he’d sent an email to Dean Clearwater requesting a meeting. The man had fallen over himself to schedule it that afternoon, but Arthur hadn’t wanted to interrupt his work with Maggie. Or, if he was being honest with himself, tell her why he was meeting with the dean. He knew Maggie didn’t want him to talk to Dean Clearwater about the budget mistake, but after she told him exactly what Evan had done, he couldn’t stop thinking about how his mistake had made her feel small. She didn’t need to fulfill some bargain, shouldn’t need to wait for the next semester to confirm that she would get her money again. He needed to fix this, and he needed to fix it now.


Edna greeted him warmly as he entered the administrative suite. “He’s wrapping up a phone call, but he’ll be ready for you in a moment.” He nodded, sitting in one of the leather seats in the waiting area. He leaned his head back, feeling all the hours he hadn’t slept the night before.


“How are things going with Maggie?”


Well, that woke him up. He looked over at Edna, who had a grin on her face that he might call mischievous. “Fine,” he said. “Why do you ask?”


“I heard she was helping you with your little problem,” Edna said, waving a hand in the general direction of Ilex Hall.


That’s one way of putting it, Arthur thought.


“I’ve always liked that girl.”


He smiled; he couldn’t help it. “Me, too.”


She winked at him, just as Dean Clearwater opened his door and waved Arthur inside. As Arthur sat down, he began explaining to Dean Clearwater why he was there. “I know I owe you a report of our dissipation efforts, but there is something else I’d like to discuss first.”


“Certainly,” Dean Clearwater said, folding his hands and looking at Arthur intently.


“It’s come to my attention that there was a significant error that happened during my oversight of the budget committee.”


Dean Clearwater frowned. “Arthur, the budget has already been approved by the board of trustees. I’ve considered this matter settled for months.”


“I’m aware, but I need to make this right. The error was completely my own. We need to open the budget again and see if there is anywhere else we can divert funds from.”


The dean’s frown deepened, and Arthur felt suddenly unsure. He hadn’t expected the pushback from the dean, but so much of the administrative ins and outs of the college were a mystery to him.


“Diverting money from elsewhere will only underfund or defund another project. There is simply no more money in the budget to move around.”


Arthur leaned forward. “Then I will fund it. Surely I can give an anonymous grant to the project?”


“That’s your prerogative, of course. You can donate any sum of money and earmark it for a specific project.” Dean Clearwater clicked a pen and shuffled through his belongings until he found a notepad. “There will be some paperwork to complete, of course. I can ask Edna to get it prepared for you. What is the program you want to fund?”


Arthur hesitated. “Dr. Linden’s senior seminar trip. Twelve thousand dollars.”


Dean Clearwater clicked the pen again and didn’t write anything down. He looked at Arthur over his glasses. “This is highly unusual. Did Dr. Linden say—”


“No,” Arthur interrupted. “She simply told me that her project was defunded for the coming year, which I found strange considering its academic merits. I looked back at the records myself and realized the error.”


The dean sighed. “Very well. If you would like to move forward with the grant, we’ll get the paperwork to you.”


“Yes. I would,” Arthur said with finality. Eager to change the subject once the matter of the paperwork was settled, Arthur gave the dean his report on the status of the pall. “The unusual strength of the pall seems to be due to a planetary conjunction occurring above the confluence of rivers in the Wilds, near Ilex Hall. We’ve narrowed our research down to a plant called a gloaming creeper that has been used to counteract the effects of the confluence on spellwork,” he explained. “We are working with Dr. Silva in the botany department on the decoction, but according to her guidance, it will be three and a half weeks before the decoction is ready. During that time, Dr. Linden will be adjusting the incantation and I the arcania to reflect the confluence.”


Satisfied with his report, Dean Clearwater dismissed him and told him to return the next day to retrieve the paperwork he needed to establish the grant for Maggie’s capstone. As he walked through campus toward Ulmus Hall, he felt lighter knowing that Maggie would be able to enroll students in the spring semester for her seminar, that she’d be able to travel to Branagh’s yew field and finish her translation of Branagh’s Aubade.


But he also knew she’d be less than pleased by his intrusion. He decided to wait until the budget was sorted, the paperwork for the grant complete, and the funding turned over to the school before he told her.


The botany lab in Ulmus Hall was on the other side of the building from the greenhouses. It was a circular, domed building whose roof and walls were constructed of glass panels that could be opened up to the sky with long levers. Decoctions sometimes required time beneath the midday sun or a waning crescent moon to reach their full power, and, with the panels, the finicky liquids could be left in the relative safety of the lab while still being exposed to the appropriate celestial enhancements.


Someone had cranked open the panel that allowed in a cross breeze, so Arthur could see through the lab as he walked up. Maggie was already inside, her hair tied up in a prim bun and safety goggles around her neck. He stood outside, watching her for a moment as she arranged cucurbits and alembics onto their reserved workstation.


When she looked up, she caught Arthur’s eyes through the open panel, and her face brightened, a wide smile breaking across her lips as she waved. The smile he returned to her probably looked goofy, a big, sloppy grin that he should try to hide a little better. He knew he had a reputation for being a grump at work, but he had learned early on that there had to be a Work Arthur. To get the kinds of results he was trained to expect out of himself, his work had to be above everything else. It had been exhausting, and coming to Hawthorn was a way to untangle that, but it hadn’t been as easy as he thought. His old habits were hard to break.


The lab had a distinct herbal and medicinal smell that stung Arthur’s nose and eyes. He’d get used to it in a few minutes, he knew, but he blinked back tears as the strong odor of various decoctions brewing in the lab hit him. He walked through the lab until he stood across from Maggie at the table she had carefully organized. She pulled out the sample box Dr. Silva had given them to collect the gloaming creeper and laid it gently beside the instruments.


Maggie looked up at him with a hesitant, almost shy expression.


He understood—what if whatever magic that had happened between them broke when they left her apartment this morning? He wanted to come around the table and cast away her doubts with a kiss, but they were not alone. He heard Dr. Silva or one of her assistants in the supply room, humming a tune along with a radio, and he was determined to follow Maggie’s rules.


“Was there much traffic?” she asked, a small smile on her face as she fumbled with a beaker, moving it away from the alembic she’d set it under. “I thought you’d never get here.”


“The beach roads are busy this time of year,” he said, his tongue darting out to lick his lips. “I came as fast as I could.”


Her smirk broadened into a wide, wicked smile. “Is that so?”


Arthur reached across the table and set his hand over hers on the beaker, stroking the spot where her palm curved into her wrist. He dragged the beaker back under the alembic. “This needs to be here.”


She watched his fingers moving on her wrist, flicking her eyes over to the supply room. “Hmm, I must have been distracted by something.”


There was the soft tap of heels on the old tile floor, and Maggie pulled her hand away from Arthur’s so fast, it was like she’d been burned. The beaker twirled and tipped over the edge of the lab table, but Arthur reached out and caught it easily.


“Oh! Excellent catch, Dr. Taliesin,” Dr. Silva gasped. “Shattered glass certainly would have put a damper on the morning.”


Maggie glared at him, her cheeks flushed. It was a familiar expression, one he’d felt boring into his back for weeks before their agreement. It was almost like seeing an old friend, and he tried, very hard, to keep from grinning.


“You started it,” he mouthed across the table, but she looked away from him, focusing instead on Dr. Silva, who was now adjusting the beaker back under the equipment.


Maggie busied herself with unzipping the collection kit and removing the gloaming creeper. She untwisted the small tube of water that they had clasped around the stem to keep the vine fresh, discarding it in the sink.


“A perfect specimen,” Dr. Silva cheered. “I hope it wasn’t too difficult to retrieve.”


Maggie’s eyes shot back up to Arthur. It was a look that let him know she was replaying every moment of their time in the Wilds just like he was. “Not at all,” he said. “It was right where you told us it would be.”


Dr. Silva scanned their table and the supplies they’d arranged to begin prepping the decoction. “It looks like you have almost everything you need to get started. Did you have a chance to review the decoction procedure?”


Arthur nodded. They had looked over it together in Maggie’s bed the night before, discussing the finer points of the step-by-step instructions Dr. Silva had carefully explained to them. It was several pages long and, unfortunately, a three-and-a-half week process to transform the plant into a spell-magnifying liquid that could be combined with chalk and chalk paint to cancel out the effect of the river confluence on the pall.


“Is there anything we can do to speed up the process?” Arthur asked, already knowing the answer.


“Don’t worry, Dr. Taliesin. I know that we are racing against time here and that the pall is growing stronger every day,” she said sympathetically. “This process normally takes four weeks, but I’ve shortened the steps as much as I can without compromising the decoction. You’re incredibly lucky that the waning crescent moon is in two nights’ time. Otherwise, we could have been twiddling our thumbs for weeks waiting for the moon to be in position.”


Maggie pulled her safety goggles over her eyes and leaned down over the equipment on the table. She pressed her finger to the rune on the burner while muttering the Diadhan word for ignite. The burner burst to life.


Dr. Silva stayed for a moment to watch their progress, asking about the pall and its strange characteristics. Maggie answered while she worked, but Arthur anxiously began filling a bulbous alembic with water from the sink at the center of the table. He didn’t want to talk about the pall’s growing strength. He couldn’t stomach the thought that all of his time with Maggie, whatever she would deign to give him, would be spent on campus, babysitting the decoction and reinforcing wards all while the pall grew more dangerous. And he had no one to blame but himself. Guilt and frustration coiled in his gut.


“Thank you for all your help on this,” Maggie said to Dr. Silva as the professor returned to her office. “I promise we’ll get over to your house this week to reinforce those wards.”


He was still lost in thought when he heard Maggie tsk. He looked over at her as she began dividing the leaves from the gloaming creeper, plucking them one by one from the twisting vine. Some of his worries disappeared as he watched her methodical work. “Yes? Is there something you’d like to say?” he asked.


“I just see some flagrant disregard for lab safety.” She nudged a pair of safety glasses with her elbow. “Wear them.”


He reached across the table and put them on over his glasses. “Be careful, Maggie,” he said, his voice low. He was certain Dr. Silva couldn’t hear them over the flame of the burner and the rolling bubble of the boiling water. “I like it when you order me around, too.”
